paras: The lynching of Tom Roof took place in Trenton, Georgia, in March 1888, when a mob took a Black man accused of an attempted assault on Mrs. Joseph Morrison from the county jail and hanged him in the public square. Papers across the country carried the story, giving the man's name variously as Roof, Root, Poof and Ruffin. Much of the coverage turned on one wire's claim that the mob "consisted mostly of women."

According to the Savannah Morning News, the accused assaulted Mrs. Joe Morrison at "Diemont Hill" on a Tuesday evening but "failed in his purpose and escaped." He was arrested in Chattanooga on Thursday and brought to Trenton on Friday. There he was committed to jail in default of $5,000 bond.

Most wire versions place the lynching on Saturday night, March 10. A mob came to the jail and overpowered Sheriff Byrd, as one wire spelled his name, who delivered the keys "to save the jail from being demolished." A later dispatch, which spelled the name Bird, said instead that he "resisted the mob to the last" before he was forced to surrender the keys.

The mob took the prisoner to the public square and hanged him from a rafter of the shed there. The Savannah dispatch described the attackers as "an armed mob" and said he was hung "until he was dead." Both wire versions asserted that Roof admitted his guilt or confessed just before he was lynched, without naming who heard the confession.
No report of an inquest, arrests or a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News, the only Georgia paper in the coverage, ran its own Trenton dispatch on March 11 under the headline "Short Shift to a Flend [Fiend]." Associated wire versions appeared the next day in St. Paul, Omaha, Indianapolis, Fort Worth, Sacramento, Los Angeles and Unionville, Nevada. Their headlines ranged from the plain "A Negro Hanged" and "Hanged Without a Trial" to "COLORED RAVISHER LYNCHED" and "A Black Fiend Lynched." The Fort Worth Gazette's subhead, "A Negro Who Confessed to a Criminal Assault," presented the confession claim as settled.

A second wire dated March 12 ran as "Lynched by Women" in weeklies in Minnesota, Wisconsin, Ohio and Dakota through March 23. A boiled-down version in the weekly news summaries reduced the case to a single line about a man "lynched by a mob of women." The Maysville Evening Bulletin turned the item into a jest, writing that "Fair girls and spectacled mothers" had "vindicated the honor of Mrs. Joe Morrison and the female sex." No editorial objecting to the lynching was found in the coverage.

The papers disagreed on the victim's name: most wires printed Tom Roof, one gave Tom Root and Roof in successive sentences, another printed Tom Poof, and the Savannah dispatch called him Tom Ruffin. The date also varies, since the Savannah dispatch, dated March 10, says the hanging took place "last night," while an Elko, Nevada, paper rewrote the wire to say "Sunday night."

Only the March 12 wire and items drawn from it said the mob was mostly women. The Savannah report spoke of "an armed mob," and the Los Angeles Herald's copy of the earlier wire reads that he was hanged "by men."

reader.title: Lynching of Tom Roof
bases: A mob took a Black prisoner accused of an attempted assault on a white woman from the Trenton jail and hanged him in the public square (A1, A3, A14).
Every account says a mob took the accused man from jail before any trial and hanged him until dead (A1, A9, A14); the mob acted to punish an alleged assault on Mrs. Joseph Morrison (A3, A11).

A separate Savannah Morning News dispatch (A1) and the Associated wire versions (A3, A14) agree on the arrest in Chattanooga, the jail seizure and the public-square hanging, while differing on the name and some details.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News dispatch
accounts.gist: Tom Ruffin assaulted Mrs. Morrison at Diemont Hill Tuesday, failed and escaped, was arrested in Chattanooga, held in default of $5,000 bond and taken by an armed mob and hanged on the square.

accounts.label: Wire report (March 11)
accounts.gist: Tom Roof, who 'attempted criminal assault' on Mrs. Morrison, was hanged in the public square; he 'admitted his guilt' and Sheriff Byrd gave up the keys after a 'show of resistance'.

accounts.label: Wire report (March 12)
accounts.gist: Roof was hanged from a shed rafter Saturday night; Sheriff Bird resisted 'to the last'; Roof confessed just before the lynching; the mob was mostly women.

framing.detail: Headlines named him a 'COLORED RAVISHER' and 'A Black Fiend' and stated the accusation and a confession as fact.
The Maysville Evening Bulletin treated it as a quip: 'Fair girls and spectacled mothers' vindicated 'the honor' of Mrs. Morrison 'and the female sex'.
Most papers ran a one-sentence wire or weekly-summary item without comment, some under 'Lynched by Women' or 'Hanged Without a Trial'.
